name: St. John Cathedral Oak

location.address: Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist, 515 Cathedral St, Lafayette, LA 70501

official_register.name: Live Oak Society (Louisiana Garden Club Federation), charter member of 1934

verify_notes: Charter member of the Live Oak Society (founded 1934 by Dr Edwin L. Age: estimates differ and are all vague. Lafayette Travel (Sept 2025): 'some estimates place the tree's age at more than 450 years'; 100oaks: more than 450; cathedral says the tree was about 275 years old in 1821, which would put it near 475 now; Waymarking says 500; Stephens' 1934 girth method gave about 150 years, which the sources treat as far too low. story:
Lafayette's cathedral may stand where it does because of this tree. When Jean Mouton gave the land in 1821, the parish's first pastor, Michel Bernard Barrière, may have asked for this exact spot because of the oak, by the cathedral's own telling.

It was old even then. The cathedral reckoned it about 275 years old at the time. Lafayette Travel and the 100oaks blog now put it past 450, and Waymarking says 500. These are estimates, not ring counts, and the low outlier shows how loose they are. In 1934 Dr Edwin Stephens' girth method gave it about 150 years, which the same sources treat as far too low.

Stephens founded the Live Oak Society that year, and this oak was one of its 43 charter members. He liked to pose in front of it and put it at the top of his Live Oak Trail tours. It now holds office in the Society, as second vice president.

The tape measure tells a stranger story. Stephens recorded 19 feet around in about 1929. Arborist Jim Foret measured 28 feet 8 inches in 2008 and 29 feet 6 inches in 2015, about nine metres. Some of that jump is how people measured. Foret also thinks the care since the 1990s helped, when the parking lot was moved away and, in 1995, a fence went up around the roots.

The fence stays, so you see it from the cathedral grounds.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fence around its roots, put up in 1995, and a trunk about nine metres round. It stands on the cathedral grounds, roughly 60 metres to the left of the front entrance.

name: Evangeline Oak

story:
Louisiana's most famous oak is not especially old and not especially big. Both Lafayette Travel and the 100oaks blog say so, and both send you here anyway, because people come for a love story.

Longfellow's Evangeline tells of Acadian lovers parted in exile, but the poem never puts them under this tree. That came later, in 1907, when Judge Felix Voorhies' Acadian Reminiscences set the reunion of Emmeline Labiche and Louis Arceneaux, held by tradition to be the real Evangeline and Gabriel, under an oak on Bayou Teche. The state plaque beside this trunk makes the link today. By some accounts this is the third oak in the area to be named as the one, which says a good deal about how badly people wanted a tree for the story.

It has needed rescuing in its own right. In 2019 an arborist and the LSU AgCenter warned the city council that fig vines were strangling it, and by local press accounts the vines were cleared in 2022.

It stands in Evangeline Oak Park at the foot of East Port Street, on the bank of the bayou, with a boardwalk alongside and the Old Castillo next door. Nobody has published its age or its girth. If you know either, tell us.

St. Martinville is a day trip from Lafayette, about half an hour by car to the southeast.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the state plaque and the chain posts around it, at the bayou's edge at the foot of East Port Street. It stands in Evangeline Oak Park, next to the Old Castillo.

name: Twentieth Century Oaks

location.address: University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Johnston St at University Ave (near Girard Hall), Lafayette, LA 70504

access: Free. Open campus along Johnston Street; the oaks line the walkways near Girard Hall.
transport: UL Lafayette campus, just south of downtown Lafayette on Johnston Street. Bus stop not checked.
verify_notes: Not ancient: a documented planting. Dr Edwin L. Stephens, aged 27 and the first president of Southwestern Louisiana Institute, planted 18 young live oaks on New Year's Day 1901 near the campus entrance at Johnston St and University Ave and named them the Twentieth Century Oaks. Age is derived from that date (about 125 years, 2026). Survivors: Lafayette Travel (Sept 2025) and 100oaks say ten still stand, near Girard Hall; The Advocate (search summary only, not fetched) says eight, so the count is disputed: state 'about eight to ten'. Grounds manager Mike Hess cares for them among 250+ campus live oaks. Their link to the story: Stephens founded the Live Oak Society in 1934 and took 25 acorns a year from member trees as dues to grow young oaks for the campus; a 2014 bronze statue of Stephens holding an acorn stands near the Century Oaks and Girard Hall; a historical marker stands at the Johnston/University intersection (hmdb m=111638 not readable, 403). No girth figure found, so no girth_cm. Ensemble with one place to stand (the Girard Hall walkway); position is Girard Hall (OSM way 462617385, 30.21647, -92.01934), approximate, campus-level, no small-site claim. Commons has 'Century Oak.jpg' (a UL Lafayette 1900 planting), licence not checked. Weakest of the three: young by tree standards, historically significant.
story:
On New Year's Day 1901 a 27-year-old college president planted eighteen young live oaks at his campus entrance and named them for the century that had just begun. Dr Edwin L. Stephens was the first president of Southwestern Louisiana Institute, now the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, and these are his Twentieth Century Oaks.

By live oak standards they are young, about 125 years old, and size is not the reason to come. History is. The man who planted them went on to found the Live Oak Society in 1934, a register whose members are trees, and he set its dues at 25 acorns a year from each member, to grow young oaks for the campus. The grounds staff now look after more than 250 live oaks there.

How many of the original eighteen survive depends on who is counting. Lafayette Travel and the 100oaks blog say ten, while The Advocate has reported eight. Call it eight to ten, standing along the walkways near Girard Hall.

Since 2014 a bronze Stephens has stood close by, holding an acorn, and a historical marker stands at Johnston Street and University Avenue, near where he planted them. Come for the founder and his New Year's planting more than for the trees themselves, and the walk repays it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the live oaks along the walkways near Girard Hall, with the 2014 bronze statue of Edwin Stephens holding an acorn close by. They stand near Johnston Street and University Avenue.
